title: Reading minds using brain scans, with Kenneth Norman, PhD

sentences.en: The idea of a machine that can read your mind sounds more like science fiction than actual science.
sentences.zh: 能够读取人脑思维的机器，听起来更像是科幻小说而非现实科学。

sentences.en: After all, what could be more private and inaccessible to the outside world than what goes on in your own head?
sentences.zh: 毕竟，还有什么比你脑子里正在想的事情更私密、更无法被外界触及的呢？

sentences.en: But in recent years, scientists have been coming closer to making this fantastical-seeming idea into reality.
sentences.zh: 但近年来，科学家们正越来越接近将这个看似奇幻的想法变为现实。

sentences.en: They've developed brain-scanning tools and methods that can interpret brain activity, and from that activity, decode many aspects of what people are thinking.
sentences.zh: 他们开发了能够解读大脑活动的脑部扫描工具和方法，并能从这些活动中解码出人们思维的许多方面。

sentences.en: in essence, reading their minds.
sentences.zh: 本质上，就是读取他们的思想。

sentences.en: So how does this technology work?
sentences.zh: 那么这项技术是如何运作的呢？

sentences.en: How do scientists translate patterns of brain activity into thoughts?
sentences.zh: 科学家们是如何将大脑活动的模式转化为思想的？

sentences.en: What kinds of thoughts can they decode?
sentences.zh: 他们能解码出什么样的思想？

sentences.en: How advanced are these methods?
sentences.zh: 这些方法有多先进？

sentences.en: And what are the limitations?
sentences.zh: 又有哪些局限性？

sentences.en: What research questions can they help scientists to answer?
sentences.zh: 它们能帮助科学家回答哪些研究问题？

sentences.en: What practical and moral questions does this research raise?
sentences.zh: 这项研究引发了哪些实际和道德层面的问题？

sentences.en: And where might it be going in the future.
sentences.zh: 未来它又将向何处发展？

sentences.en: Welcome to Speaking of Psychology, the flagship podcast of the
sentences.zh: 欢迎收听《心理学对话》，这是美国心理学会的旗舰播客，

sentences.en: American Psychological Association that examines the links between psychological science and everyday life.
sentences.zh: 旨在探讨心理科学与日常生活之间的联系。

sentences.en: I'm Kim Mills.
sentences.zh: 我是主持人金·米尔斯。

sentences.en: My guest today is Dr. Kenneth Norman, a professor of psychology and neuroscience and chair of the psychology department at Princeton University.
sentences.zh: 今天的嘉宾是肯尼斯·诺曼博士，他是普林斯顿大学心理学与神经科学教授，也是心理学系主任。

sentences.en: In his lab, the Princeton Computational Memory Lab, he and his colleagues developed new methods to analyze brain scans.
sentences.zh: 在他的实验室——普林斯顿计算记忆实验室，他和同事们开发了分析脑部扫描的新方法。

sentences.en: They use those methods to study learning and memory by decoding people's thoughts as they learn and remember.
sentences.zh: 他们利用这些方法，通过解码人们学习和记忆时的思维来研究学习与记忆。

sentences.en: He has published more than 100 research papers and his work has been funded by the National Institutes of Health and the National Science Foundation, among others.
sentences.zh: 他发表了100多篇研究论文，其工作得到了美国国立卫生研究院和国家科学基金会等机构的资助。

sentences.en: Dr. Norman also teaches an undergraduate class called fMRI decoding, reading minds using brain scans.
sentences.zh: 诺曼博士还教授一门名为“fMRI解码：利用脑部扫描读取思维”的本科课程。

sentences.en: And he has won several awards for his mentoring and teaching.
sentences.zh: 他曾多次获得教学与指导方面的奖项。

sentences.en: Thank you for joining me today, Dr. Norman.
sentences.zh: 感谢您今天参加节目，诺曼博士。

sentences.en: I'm looking forward to talking about this fascinating research.
sentences.zh: 我很期待讨论这项迷人的研究。

sentences.en: I'm very happy to be here.
sentences.zh: 很高兴来到这里。

sentences.en: Thanks.
sentences.zh: 谢谢。

sentences.en: I mentioned in the introduction that the whole topic can sound like science fiction or even a parlor game, for that matter, to people who aren't familiar with it.
sentences.zh: 我在开场白中提到，对于不熟悉的人来说，整个话题听起来可能像科幻小说，甚至像某种派对游戏。

sentences.en: So let's start by getting some basic grounding in the science.
sentences.zh: 那么，让我们先从科学基础开始了解。

sentences.en: Can you explain in a fairly non-technical way how this works?
sentences.zh: 您能用一种相当通俗易懂的方式解释一下它是如何运作的吗？

sentences.en: When we say you're working on reading minds, what does that mean and what are the tools that you're using?
sentences.zh: 当我们说您正在从事“读取思维”的研究时，这意味着什么？您使用的工具又是什么？

sentences.en: The core idea is that different thoughts correspond to different patterns of neural firing in our brain.
sentences.zh: 核心思想是：不同的思想对应着我们大脑中不同的神经放电模式。

sentences.en: So if we want to be able to decode people's thoughts, we need to be able to pick up on, for example, the difference in the pattern of neural firing associated with
sentences.zh: 因此，如果我们想要解码人们的思想，就需要能够捕捉到，例如，与

sentences.en: you thinking about a strawberry or a frog or a tree or what have you.
sentences.zh: 你思考草莓、青蛙、树木或其他任何事物时相关联的神经放电模式差异。

sentences.en: And so the way we do this is with MRI machines.
sentences.zh: 我们实现这一目标的方式是使用核磁共振（MRI）机器。

sentences.en: And so when people talk about functional MRI, basically we're talking about tuning an MRI machine to detect brain activity.
sentences.zh: 当人们谈论功能性核磁共振（fMRI）时，基本上我们是在谈论如何调整核磁共振机器来检测大脑活动。

sentences.en: And the way we do that is by tuning it to detect levels of blood oxygen.
sentences.zh: 我们实现这一目标的方法是将其调整为检测血液中的氧含量水平。

sentences.en: And basically, the idea is that parts of the brain that are more active use up more oxygen from the blood.
sentences.zh: 基本原理是：大脑中更活跃的区域会消耗血液中更多的氧气。

sentences.en: So if we've tuned the MRI machine to detect that, we can get a sense of which parts of your brain are more active than other parts of the brain.
sentences.zh: 因此，如果我们调整核磁共振机器来检测这一点，就能感知到你大脑中哪些部分比其他部分更活跃。

sentences.en: And so this is a very indirect measure of neural firing.
sentences.zh: 所以，这是一种对神经放电非常间接的测量。

sentences.en: We're not picking up on the electrical zapping of neurons.
sentences.zh: 我们捕捉到的并不是神经元的电脉冲。

sentences.en: We're picking up on this kind of blood flow correlate of neural zapping.
sentences.zh: 我们捕捉到的是这种与神经脉冲相关的血流变化。

sentences.en: And so it's really an open question whether the signal we're getting out of this specially tuned MRI machine is going to be too blurry to detect these sort of nuanced differences in neural firing or whether it will be resolved enough to be able to do that.
sentences.zh: 因此，我们从这台特殊调整的核磁共振机器中获得的信号是否会因为过于模糊而无法检测到神经放电中那种细微的差异，或者它是否足够清晰以至于能够做到这一点，这确实是一个悬而未决的问题。

sentences.en: And so that's sort of the game that we've been playing has been trying to figure out whether this imperfect carload neural firing can pick up on these relatively subtle neural patterns.
sentences.zh: 所以，我们一直在玩的游戏就是试图弄清楚这种不完美的神经放电相关指标是否能够捕捉到这些相对微妙的神经模式。

sentences.en: And to cut to the chase, the answer is it does it surprisingly well.
sentences.zh: 长话短说，答案是它做得出奇地好。

sentences.en: Right.
sentences.zh: 没错。

sentences.en: And so the way that we do brain decoding is basically we ask people to think about one thing so we can ask them to think about frogs.
sentences.zh: 我们进行大脑解码的方式基本上是要求人们思考某件事，比如我们可以让他们思考青蛙。

sentences.en: right and we take a bunch of snapshots of their brain activity with the mri machine while they're
sentences.zh: 对，我们在他们思考青蛙时，用核磁共振机器拍摄大量他们大脑活动的快照，

sentences.en: thinking about frogs and then we could ask them to think about lizards and we could take a bunch
sentences.zh: 然后我们可以让他们思考蜥蜴，我们可以在他们思考蜥蜴时拍摄大量

sentences.en: of snapshots of their brain activity when they think about lizards and then we feed those snapshots
sentences.zh: 他们大脑活动的快照，然后我们将这些快照——

sentences.en: the frog snapshots and the lizard snapshots into a computer program that has basically been
sentences.zh: 青蛙的快照和蜥蜴的快照——输入到一个计算机程序中，该程序基本上已经

sentences.en: optimized to try to find the differences in the patterns of brain activity, sort of which brain areas are more or less active when you're thinking about frogs or lizards, right?
sentences.zh: 经过优化，试图找出大脑活动模式中的差异，即当你思考青蛙或蜥蜴时，哪些大脑区域更活跃或更不活跃，对吧？

sentences.en: That's what a pattern classifier is, right?
sentences.zh: 这就是模式分类器的作用，对吧？

sentences.en: It's a machine learning algorithm that is basically trying to find opportunistically any difference in the patterns that you feed it.
sentences.zh: 它是一种机器学习算法，基本上是在试图机会性地找出你输入给它的模式中的任何差异。

sentences.en: And so if there's a reliable difference in the frog pattern and lizard pattern, it'll find it.
sentences.zh: 所以，如果青蛙模式和蜥蜴模式之间存在可靠的差异，它就能找到。

sentences.en: So if you and I were both put into an MRI machine and were told to think about frogs, would our patterns look essentially the same?
sentences.zh: 那么，如果我们俩都被放入核磁共振机器中，并被告知思考青蛙，我们的模式看起来会基本相同吗？

sentences.en: They would look kind of similar, right?
sentences.zh: 它们看起来会有点相似，对吧？

sentences.en: But not identical because you and I might have had different life experiences with frogs and lizards, right?
sentences.zh: 但不会完全相同，因为你我对于青蛙和蜥蜴可能有过不同的生活经历，对吧？

sentences.en: And the way that our brain represents thing is a function of our personal experience.
sentences.zh: 而我们大脑表征事物的方式正是我们个人经历的函数。

sentences.en: But the idea is that our experiences will have been similar enough that there should be some transfer between my brain patterns and your brain patterns.
sentences.zh: 但我们的想法是，我们的经历应该足够相似，以至于我的大脑模式和你的大脑模式之间应该存在某种迁移。

sentences.en: And concretely, what that means is that if you train one of these pattern classifier algorithms on the frog versus lizard distinction in my brain, right, it'll do the best
sentences.zh: 具体来说，这意味着如果你在我的大脑中针对“青蛙与蜥蜴”的区别训练了其中一种模式分类算法，对吧，它在解码我关于青蛙与蜥蜴的思想时会做得最好，对吧？

sentences.en: job at decoding my frog versus lizard thoughts, right?
sentences.zh: 但它在检测你关于青蛙与蜥蜴的思想时，可能仍然会高于随机水平，对吧？

sentences.en: But it'll still possibly be above chance, right, at detecting your frog versus lizard thoughts.
sentences.zh: 我是说，在我看来，人脑之间相似性最显著的例子是我实验室里的一位前博士后，她现在已经是教员了，

sentences.en: I mean, the most striking example to me of similarity across people's brains was a former postdoc in my lab who's now a faculty
sentences.zh: 叫珍妮丝·陈。

sentences.en: John Topkins.
sentences.zh: 珍妮丝·陈在普林斯顿工作时进行了一项研究，她在人们观看本尼迪克特·康伯巴奇主演的《神探夏洛克》电视剧整集时对他们进行了扫描。

sentences.en: Janice Chen, when she was here at Princeton, ran a study where she scanned people while they watched an entire episode of the Benedict Cumberbatch Sherlock TV series.
sentences.zh: 然后，她让他们在扫描仪中回忆刚才看的内容，同时扫描他们的大脑。

sentences.en: And then she had them just recall it in the scanner while their brains were being scanned.
sentences.zh: 她对很多人都做了这项实验。

sentences.en: And she did this for a bunch of people.
sentences.zh: 她所展示的结果在当时让我们感到非常震惊，那就是你可以训练这些模式分类器来解码一个人正在观看电视剧的哪一集场景。

sentences.en: And what she showed, which was totally amazing to us at the time is that you could train one of these pattern classifiers to decode which scene of the TV
sentences.zh: 所以她根据我的大脑训练它来解码这是剧中的哪个场景。

sentences.en: episode a person was watching.
sentences.zh: 然后她证明了它在迁移到其他人的大脑时表现得非常好，对吧？

sentences.en: So she trained it to decode based on my brain, which scene of the episode it was.
sentences.zh: 因此，用于表征这部电视剧中特定场景的代码——这看起来是一件相当精细的事情——似乎在不同人之间是通用的，

sentences.en: And then she showed that it did an incredibly good job at transferring to other people's brains, right?
sentences.zh: 这并不是我们所预料到的。

sentences.en: So the code that's being used to represent a particular scene in this TV episode, which seems like a fairly fine-grained thing, appears to be common across people,
sentences.zh: 核磁共振成像技术已经存在几十年了，至少从90年代初就开始了。

sentences.en: which is not what we expected.
sentences.zh: 近年来有什么变化使得您的工作成为可能？

sentences.zh: 有两件事发生了变化，对吧？

sentences.zh: 一件事是机器输出信号的质量。

sentences.en: There are two things that could change, right?

sentences.en: One thing is sort of the quality of the signal coming out of the machine.
sentences.zh: 这两方面都发生了变化，但使这种思维解码成为可能的主要创新是在分析方面，对吧？

sentences.en: And the other thing is how we analyze the data.
sentences.zh: 我们在处理和分析数据的方式上比过去要复杂得多。

sentences.en: And so both those things have changed, but the main innovations that have made this kind of thought decoding possible are on the analysis side, right?
sentences.zh: 你知道，其中一部分原因仅仅是计算机速度更快了，

sentences.en: We're much more sophisticated in how we kind of chew on and analyze the data than we used to be.
sentences.zh: 人们开发出了更好的模式分类算法。但部分原因是我们从概念上以不同的方式来处理它。

sentences.en: You know, some of it is just like computers are faster and

sentences.zh: 有很多不同的动物，对吧？

sentences.zh: 有成百上千种，对吧？

sentences.zh: 所以解决这个问题的一种方法是，我可以尝试为每种动物训练一个单独的思维解码器。

sentences.zh: 所以我可以让你思考熊，然后思考“非熊”的事物。

sentences.zh: 我们的想法是，我们可以为每一个属性训练一个不同的解码器，对吧？

sentences.en: They could be dangerous or not dangerous, right?
sentences.zh: 所以我们可以在你思考大型动物和小型动物时拍摄大脑快照，对吧？

sentences.en: And the idea is that we could train a different decoder for each of those attributes, right?
sentences.zh: 或者陆地动物或水生动物，对吧？

sentences.en: So we could sort of take brain snapshots while you're thinking of big animals and small animals, right?
sentences.zh: 我们的想法是，动物变化的维度数量，对吧，是，你知道，超过三个，对吧？

sentences.en: Or land animals or water animals, right?
sentences.zh: 但少于一千个，对吧？

sentences.zh: 所以如果你想想“20个问题”这个游戏，它之所以是20个问题而不是100个问题，是因为你不需要100个问题就能弄清楚别人在说什么。
